title: Tenali Raman Tale 134

full_text:
Two cloth merchants, Madhav and Keshav, formed a business partnership to buy and sell fine silks. After a year of trading, they had accumulated fifty bolts of silk of varying quality and twenty bags of silver.
However, mutual greed corrupted their partnership:
Madhav claimed the finest twenty-five bolts of gold-embroidered silk, offering Keshav only the coarse dyed cotton;
Keshav claimed all twenty bags of silver, offering Madhav only the damaged goods.
They appeared before King Krishnadevaraya, accusing each other of embezzlement and perjury.

The King, exhausted by their shouting, asked Tenali Raman to divide the assets equitably.

Tenali smiled:
'Maharaj, ancient law provides the perfect, incorruptible method of equitable division:
**The Rule of the Cake: One Divides, the Other Chooses!**'

Tenali brought all fifty bolts of silk and the twenty bags of silver into the center of the hall.
He turned to Madhav:
'Madhav, since you claim to be the senior partner, you shall divide all the silk and silver into two separate piles upon this floor.
Divide them however you see fit!'

Madhav’s eyes gleamed with greed. He thought:
'I will put the forty finest silk bolts and fifteen bags of silver into Pile One, and put the ten cheap bolts and five bags into Pile Two, so I can claim Pile One!'
Madhav arranged the piles accordingly.

When Madhav finished, he puffed out his chest: 'The division is complete!'

Tenali Raman smiled with devastating brilliance and turned to **Keshav**:
'Now, Keshav! As the junior partner, you have the absolute legal right to choose whichever pile you desire for yourself!'

Keshav leaped forward with a joyous shout and seized **Pile One** containing forty finest silks and fifteen bags of silver!
Madhav was left staring in frozen, horrified despair at **Pile Two**, containing only ten cheap bolts and five bags!

Madhav shrieked: 'Wait! That is unfair! I made Pile One for myself!'

Tenali looked at him with stern moral justice:
'If you had divided the property with absolute fairness and equal honesty, you would have been completely satisfied with whichever pile was left!
Your own greed designed the trap, and justice has closed the door upon you!'

King Krishnadevaraya and the court cheered Tenali’s timeless demonstration of fair division.
Madhav was forced to accept his share, learning that selfish cunning always defeats its own author.
moral: Partners who conspire to cheat each other are easily exposed by requiring one to divide and the other to choose.
